platforms.name: Google Local Services Ads (LSA)
platforms.tagline: Google's pay-per-lead ads at the top of Search, with a Google Verified badge for screened businesses
platforms.typical_cost: Pay per valid lead (calls, messages, booking requests); Google publishes no rate card and says lead prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding. Moving into Google Ads as Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in phases: select US home and storefront service advertisers (including plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and pest control) from August 2026, service-area businesses without physical storefronts in late 2026, and non-US accounts and remaining categories in 2027. Manual cost-per-lead bidding is no longer supported and per-vertical Target CPAs merge into one campaign-level Target CPA; weekly budgets become daily averages.
platforms.exclusivity: Exclusive: the customer calls, messages or books your business directly through your ad
platforms.long_description:
Google Local Services Ads (LSA) are pay-per-lead ads that Google shows at the top of Search results when people look for local services such as plumbing, HVAC or roofing. A customer can call, message or send a booking request straight from the ad, and Google says you only pay when a potential customer gets in touch through it, not when someone clicks.

Before an ad runs, Google screens the business. For US home services, Google lists business and owner background checks (plus service professional checks in select categories), state-level business and owner licenses, insurance that depends on category and location, and a public, verified Google Business Profile. Google says this takes 3-4 weeks on average after you submit documents. Businesses that pass show a Google Verified badge. In 2025 Google replaced the older Google Guaranteed and Google Screened badges with this single badge and ended the money-back guarantee that came with Google Guaranteed.

Google sets lead prices and publishes no rate card: it says prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding, and that message leads are typically charged at lower rates than phone leads. Answered calls, voicemails, messages, booking requests and missed calls you follow up on can all be charged. Google says it does not charge for leads it judges invalid, re-reviews charged leads and may credit low-quality ones automatically, usually within 30 days, and lets US and Canadian advertisers dispute leads. It no longer credits leads for a job type or area you do not serve.

LSA is being folded into Google Ads. Google says local services campaigns become Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in phases: select US home and storefront service advertisers (including plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and pest control) from August 2026, service-area businesses without storefronts in late 2026, and non-US accounts and remaining categories in 2027. After migration, manual cost-per-lead bidding goes away, weekly budgets become daily averages, the old LSA dashboard redirects to Google Ads, and past performance reports are no longer available, so Google advises downloading them first. Past leads carry over to the Google Ads Leads page.

The trade-off: LSA puts a screened listing at the top of Google and bills per contact rather than per click, but you accept Google's pricing, a few weeks of screening, charges for missed calls you return, and a mid-migration product whose bidding controls and reporting are changing.
platforms.how_it_works: Set up a Local Services profile with your business details, service types and service area, set a budget, and complete Google's screening (background, license and insurance checks that vary by category and location, plus a verified Google Business Profile). Once live, your ad can appear at the top of Google Search for local customers, and they call, message or send a booking request through it. You are charged per lead, not per click: answered calls, voicemails, messages, booking requests and missed calls you follow up on count as leads. Google does not charge for leads it judges invalid, may credit low-quality leads automatically (usually within 30 days), and lets US and Canadian advertisers dispute leads. Google says failing to answer calls or respond to messages may affect ad ranking. From August 2026 accounts move into Google Ads as Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals and a campaign-level Target CPA.

pros_detail.title: Pay per lead, not per click
pros_detail.explanation: Google says you only pay when a potential customer calls, messages or sends a booking request through your ad, and message leads are typically charged at lower rates than phone leads.

pros_detail.title: Top-of-Search placement
pros_detail.explanation: Local Services Ads appear at the top of Google Search results for local service searches, and customers can contact you straight from the ad.

pros_detail.title: Screening badge
pros_detail.explanation: Businesses that pass Google's background, license and insurance checks show a Google Verified badge. Pre-badge ads let many categories start getting leads during onboarding, ranked below fully verified providers.

pros_detail.title: Automatic credits for low-quality leads
pros_detail.explanation: Google says invalid leads are not charged and charged leads are re-reviewed, with credits for low-quality leads usually applied within 30 days. US and Canadian advertisers can also dispute a lead.

pros_detail.title: Budget you can change anytime
pros_detail.explanation: You set the budget and can adjust it whenever you want; Google caps monthly spend based on that budget.

cons_detail.title: Screening takes weeks
cons_detail.explanation: Google says US screening averages 3-4 weeks after documents are submitted, and requirements include licenses, insurance, background checks that vary by category and a verified Google Business Profile.

cons_detail.title: Google controls the price
cons_detail.explanation: There is no published rate card. Lead prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding, and after the move to Google Ads manual cost-per-lead bidding is no longer supported.

cons_detail.title: Missed calls can be billed
cons_detail.explanation: A missed call with no voicemail becomes a charged lead if you return it by text, email or call. Google no longer credits leads for a job type or area you do not serve.

cons_detail.title: Responsiveness affects ranking
cons_detail.explanation: Google says regularly failing to answer calls or respond to messages may hurt your ad ranking, which is hard for a solo operator on a job site.

cons_detail.title: Migration into Google Ads
cons_detail.explanation: From August 2026 LSA accounts move into Performance Max campaigns. The old dashboard redirects to Google Ads and past performance reports are no longer accessible, so download them before your migration date.

platforms.best_for: Licensed, insured residential service businesses (HVAC, plumbing, electrical, roofing, pest control, cleaning) with a verified Google Business Profile and someone available to answer calls and messages quickly
platforms.best_team_size: Solo operators to multi-crew shops, as long as someone can answer calls and messages promptly
platforms.weaknesses: Screening averages 3-4 weeks, Google sets lead prices with no published rate card, returned missed calls are billable, and the move into Google Ads removes manual cost-per-lead bidding and the old dashboard reports.

platform_faqs.q: How long does LSA approval take?
platform_faqs.a: Google says US screening takes 3-4 weeks on average after you submit your documents. Checks vary by category and location and can include business, owner and service professional background checks, state business and owner licenses, insurance, and a public, verified Google Business Profile.

platform_faqs.q: What does a lead cost?
platform_faqs.a: Google publishes no rate card. It says lead prices vary by your location, the job type, the type of lead and your bidding, and that message leads are typically priced lower than phone leads. You control spend through your budget.

platform_faqs.q: What counts as a charged lead?
platform_faqs.a: An answered call, a voicemail, a message, a booking request (US and Canada), or a missed call without voicemail that you follow up on by text, email or call.

platform_faqs.q: What if I get a spam lead or wrong number?
platform_faqs.a: Google says leads it judges invalid are not charged, and charged leads are re-reviewed, with credits for low-quality leads usually applied within 30 days. US and Canadian advertisers can also dispute a lead. Google no longer credits leads for a job type or area you do not serve.

platform_faqs.q: Is the Google Guarantee still offered?
platform_faqs.a: No. Google replaced the Google Guaranteed and Google Screened badges with a single Google Verified badge in 2025 and discontinued the money-back guarantee; consumers had until December 7, 2025 to submit reimbursement requests.

platform_faqs.q: What changes when LSA moves into Google Ads?
platform_faqs.a: Google is moving Local Services Ads into Google Ads as Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals: select US home and storefront advertisers from August 2026, service-area businesses without storefronts in late 2026, and other accounts in 2027. Manual cost-per-lead bidding ends, per-category Target CPAs merge into one campaign-level Target CPA, weekly budgets become daily averages, and old dashboard reports are no longer accessible, while past leads move to the Google Ads Leads page.

platforms.name: 33 Mile Radius
platforms.tagline: Exclusive pay-per-call leads for restoration, roofing and other home service contractors, now part of EverConnect
platforms.typical_cost: Flat rate per valid lead that varies by service area; prices not published (quote from sales). Billed weekly; no setup fees, monthly fees or long-term contracts
platforms.exclusivity: Exclusive: each call goes to one partner contractor
platforms.long_description:
33 Mile Radius is a pay-per-call lead service for home service and restoration contractors. It says it generates calls through Google advertising, SEO-driven marketing websites and partner advertisers, then sends each live call to one partner contractor in that area. It says a lead is never provided to more than one partner.

The company is part of EverConnect, a group of marketing brands that also includes Best Pick Reports, Five Star Rated and Remodeling.com. EverCommerce sold EverConnect to Ignite Visibility, a San Diego digital marketing agency, on October 31, 2025. The site lists Tim Gill as President and an EverConnect address in Irvine, CA.

Coverage is broader than roofing. The site sells leads for water damage, fire damage, mold remediation, biohazard cleanup, plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing, siding, windows, gutters, pest control, flooring, lawn care, carpet cleaning, bath and kitchen remodeling, solar and home security. Onboarding starts with a 15-minute call to secure your service area, confirm your services and verify your business.

Pricing is not published. 33 Mile Radius says it charges a flat rate per lead that varies by service area, bills your card weekly for valid leads, and has no setup fees, monthly fees or long-term contracts. Its FAQ says partners average about 2-5 leads a month and that call volume varies with season, service, area and weather. All calls are recorded and can be disputed in the Partner Dashboard before the next billing cycle.

The trade-off: you get exclusive phone leads with no contract or monthly fee, but prices are quote-only, volume is modest and unpredictable, and the billing rules count some calls you never talk on (on its water damage page, unanswered calls and calls that go to voicemail are billable).
platforms.how_it_works: Start with a 15-minute call where 33 Mile Radius secures your service area, confirms the services you offer and verifies your business. It then runs Google advertising, SEO-driven marketing websites and partner advertising to generate calls, and routes each live call from a designated number to one partner in the area. You pay a flat rate per valid lead that varies by service area; your card is billed weekly. Valid-lead rules are listed per service: for roofing the caller must be the homeowner or decision-maker, need roofing work and be in your service area; for water damage, unanswered calls (4 rings or more) and calls that go to voicemail are also billable. Every call is recorded, and you can dispute a call in the Partner Dashboard before the next billing cycle. There is no contract: you can pause from the dashboard or cancel with 7 days' notice.

platforms.name: Service Direct
platforms.tagline: Pay-per-call marketplace where you set your own price per exclusive call, with no setup fee or contract
platforms.typical_cost: You set your price per call; vendor-published ranges: locksmiths $15-$75, appliance repair $22-$85, pest control $40-$195, electrician $55-$175, plumbing $60-$255, heating and air conditioning $65-$325, roofing $85-$550, mold removal $75-$650, water damage restoration $500-$2,250. No setup fee or term contract
platforms.exclusivity: Exclusive: calls from your zip codes route to you
platforms.long_description:
Service Direct is a pay-per-call lead marketplace for local service businesses, run by Sagax Media LLC out of Austin, TX. The business began in 2006 as Contractor Marketing Pros, building websites, before moving to its pay-per-call model. It is privately held and led by its co-founders, with Brian Abernethy as CEO.

The model is simple: you set your service area by zip code, pick the price you are willing to pay per call, and set a campaign schedule. Service Direct says it buys calls from publishers that use search engine marketing, directories, social media, mobile apps and offline channels such as direct mail, and routes exclusive calls to you. You can change your price or pause campaigns at any time, and there is no setup fee or term contract.

Service Direct publishes price-per-lead ranges by trade: locksmiths $15-$75, appliance repair $22-$85, pest control $40-$195, electricians $55-$175, plumbing $60-$255, heating and air conditioning $65-$325, mold removal $75-$650, roofing $85-$550 and water damage restoration $500-$2,250. It says you only pay for valid calls, not repeat callers, wrong numbers or solicitors, and its Quality Check feature uses machine learning to spot wrong numbers, job seekers, spam and out-of-area requests.

Results are tracked in the mySD dashboard, which shows calls, recordings and return on spend. Service Direct says it has delivered more than 2.4 million calls to more than 8,300 clients. It does not publish a minimum call length, a dispute window or a guaranteed call volume.

The trade-off: you control the price per call and can stop anytime with no contract, but the published ranges run high for restoration and roofing, the billing and dispute rules are not spelled out in public, and call volume depends on the price you set and demand in your area.
platforms.how_it_works: Apply online, then set your service area by zip code, choose the price per lead you are willing to pay for each service, and set a campaign schedule. Service Direct buys calls from publishers that use search engine marketing, directories, social media, mobile apps and offline channels, and routes exclusive calls to you. You only pay for valid calls: the company says repeat callers, wrong numbers and solicitors are not billable, and its Quality Check system screens for wrong numbers, job seekers, spam and out-of-area requests. You can set a monthly budget notification, change your price or pause campaigns anytime, and track calls, recordings and ROI in the mySD dashboard. There are no setup fees and no term contract.

platforms.name: CallRail
platforms.tagline: Call tracking and attribution software that shows which of your lead sources produce calls
platforms.typical_cost: $50-$195/mo billed yearly ($55-$215/mo billed monthly) across four plans, each with 5 numbers and 250 minutes; extra local numbers $3 each, local minutes $0.05-$0.06
platforms.exclusivity: Not a lead source: tracks and attributes calls, texts and forms from your other channels
platforms.long_description:
CallRail is call tracking and marketing attribution software, not a lead source. It gives you tracking phone numbers to place on each marketing channel, such as Google Ads, your Google Business Profile, Local Services Ads, directory listings, direct mail or truck wraps, so every inbound call is tied back to where it came from. CallRail was founded in 2011 in Atlanta by Andy Powell and Kevin Mann, is led by CEO Marc Ginsberg, and says more than 225,000 businesses use it.

On your website, dynamic number insertion swaps the displayed phone number based on how the visitor arrived, using a JavaScript snippet, so web-driven calls are attributed automatically. CallRail also records and routes calls, tracks texts, and on its Complete plans tracks web form submissions with a built-in form builder. Integrations listed on its site include Jobber, Housecall Pro and ServiceTitan, plus Google Ads, Google Analytics 4, Google Business Profile, HubSpot and Salesforce.

Pricing is published. There are four plans: Lead Tracking at $50 a month, Lead Tracking Complete at $95, Lead Conversion at $150 and Lead Conversion Complete at $195 on yearly billing, or $55, $105, $165 and $215 billed monthly. Each includes 5 numbers and 250 minutes; extra local numbers are $3 each and extra local minutes $0.05-$0.06. The Lead Conversion plans add Premium Conversation Intelligence features such as call summaries, sentiment analysis and automatic conversion tagging. A Voice Assist add-on for answering missed calls starts at $95 a month. There is a 14-day free trial with no credit card.

For a trade business, the value is knowing which lead sources actually produce booked jobs. If you pay for several channels at once, tracked numbers and recorded calls let you compare cost per call and outcome by source instead of guessing.

The trade-off: CallRail brings in no new leads by itself and adds a monthly subscription plus usage charges, and it takes some setup to place tracking numbers and the website snippet, but it is the piece that shows whether your paid lead sources are worth what you spend.
platforms.how_it_works: Start a 14-day free trial (no credit card) and pick a plan. Assign tracking numbers to each marketing channel: one on your Google Business Profile, one on a directory listing, one on direct mail, and so on. Add CallRail's JavaScript snippet to your website so dynamic number insertion shows each visitor a number tied to how they arrived. When a customer calls or texts, CallRail records and routes the call and attributes it to the source. Complete plans also track web form submissions. Lead Conversion plans add call summaries, sentiment analysis and automatic conversion tagging. Integrations with Jobber, Housecall Pro and ServiceTitan pass call and lead data into your field service software. Each plan includes 5 numbers and 250 minutes, with per-number and per-minute charges beyond that.

pros_detail.title: Dynamic number insertion

pros_detail.title: Published pricing and free trial

platform_faqs.q: Is CallRail a lead source?
platform_faqs.a: No. CallRail tracks and attributes calls, texts and form submissions that come from your other channels, such as Google Ads, Local Services Ads, directories or direct mail. If you need new leads, you need a lead source; CallRail tells you which of them are working.

platform_faqs.q: How much does CallRail cost?
platform_faqs.a: Lead Tracking is $50 a month, Lead Tracking Complete $95, Lead Conversion $150 and Lead Conversion Complete $195 on yearly billing, or $55, $105, $165 and $215 billed monthly. Each includes 5 numbers and 250 minutes, with extra local numbers at $3 each and local minutes at $0.05-$0.06.

platform_faqs.a: Lead Tracking covers call and text tracking, recording, routing and transcription. platforms.long_description:
Thumbtack is a local services marketplace where homeowners find and contact pros for about 500 kinds of jobs. It was founded in 2008 in San Francisco and is led by CEO and co-founder Marco Zappacosta. Its 2024 fact sheet says customers have started 80 million projects and that Thumbtack has raised more than $500 million from investors including Sequoia, Baillie Gifford, Blackstone and CapitalG. The top projects it lists are house cleaning, handyman work, appliance repair, local moving and lawn mowing.

Pros pay for leads, not for sending quotes. You set a lead price for each service you offer, and Thumbtack says that price is the exact amount you pay per lead; you can change it anytime. A weekly budget caps total spending, and once you reach it you stop getting leads until the next week. Thumbtack publishes no rate card and says what a lead is worth varies with the type and size of the job, how many pros are available and your market.

There are two ways to get work. With a direct lead, the customer finds your profile and reaches out, and you are charged at that point. With Opportunities, you see a job and its price upfront, reach out first, and pay only if the customer responds. A Thumbtack moderator has explained that some customers contact only one pro while others want more than one bid, so a paid lead is not a guaranteed job.

Thumbtack's own advice to pros is practical: tune your job preferences and budget so you only get leads you want, send a strong first message that shows your experience and reviews, and fill in your profile FAQs so customers have answers upfront.

The trade-off: you control your price per lead and your weekly spend, and Opportunities cost nothing unless the customer replies, but direct leads are charged even if the customer hires someone else or goes quiet, and some customers compare several pros.
platforms.how_it_works: Create a pro profile, choose the services and area you cover, set a lead price for each service and set a weekly budget. When a customer finds your profile and reaches out, that direct lead is charged at your lead price and comes out of your weekly budget; when the budget is used up, leads pause until the next week. You can also browse Opportunities: jobs shown with a price upfront, where you reach out first and pay only if the customer responds. Some customers contact one pro and others ask several for bids, so your profile, reviews, first message and response time help decide who gets hired. Thumbtack publishes no rate card; lead value varies by job type and size, how many pros are available and your market.

platforms.long_description:
Houzz Pro is the business software and marketing product of Houzz Inc., the home design and remodeling platform. Houzz's own timeline says Houzz officially became a company in October 2010 and launched Houzz Pro software for home professionals in April 2020. Houzz says its platform is used by more than 3 million construction and design professionals and over 70 million homeowners and home design enthusiasts, and its careers page describes the company as remote-first.

On the lead side, you build a Houzz profile with project photos and client reviews, and Houzz says pros appear in relevant searches based on location, project type and services. Homeowners can message you and book a video meeting from your profile. Houzz says its lead generation uses subscription-based pricing instead of pay-per-lead. The optional Advertising Package, which Houzz lists from $499/mo, shows your ads in Houzz search results when homeowners look for professionals and while they browse projects and professionals, targeted by the service areas, service types, project types and budget ranges you choose. Houzz's pages do not say whether ad leads go only to you or how many to expect.

The software is most of what the subscription buys. The free plan includes a 3D Floor Planner, estimates and invoicing. Design ($99/mo, 1 user) covers 3D floor plans, selections, mood boards, a CRM, estimates and proposals, invoices and online payments. Pro ($199/mo, 1 user) adds takeoffs, bid management, change orders, budget management, contracts, project schedules and daily logs. Teams (from $399/mo, unlimited users) adds AI note-taking, the Premium Profile, email marketing, a custom website and dedicated support. Extra users on Design and Pro cost $50/user/mo, and Houzz lists integrations with QuickBooks Online, calendar apps, Gmail and Zoom.

The trade-off: Houzz Pro is built around design and remodel projects, and the advertising that drives inquiries is a separate package starting at $499/mo on top of a plan. If you already run job-management software, much of the bundle may duplicate it. Houzz's pricing page says your annual subscription begins when the 30-day free trial ends, so decide during the trial and get any lead-volume or ad terms in writing.
platforms.how_it_works: Create a Houzz profile with project photos, services, service area and client reviews. Houzz says pros appear in relevant searches by location, project type and services, and homeowners can message you or book a video meeting from your profile. With the optional Advertising Package, Houzz shows your ads in its professional search results and while homeowners browse projects and professionals, targeted by the service areas, service types, project types and budget ranges you set, and notifies you (optionally by SMS) when a homeowner submits a project request through an ad. Leads land in the Houzz Pro CRM, where you can also import leads from other sources and move them through stages into estimates, proposals, contracts and invoices.

cons_detail.explanation: Houzz's pricing page says you can cancel during the 30-day free trial before your annual subscription begins at the end of the trial. Evaluate it during the trial, not after.

cons_detail.explanation: Houzz describes itself as a platform for construction and design, and tools such as 3D floor plans, mood boards and selections do little for repair or emergency-service work.

cons_detail.explanation: If you already use job-management or estimating software, the bundled CRM, estimating and invoicing tools may duplicate it. Houzz lists QuickBooks Online as an integration.

platform_faqs.a: The pricing model differs. Houzz says its lead generation uses subscription pricing rather than pay-per-lead, and its ads are sold as a monthly package. platforms.long_description:
Porch.com, Inc. is part of Porch Group, Inc. (Nasdaq: PRCH), based in Seattle. Porch says it was founded in 2012, launched in 2013 as a home services marketplace, pivoted in 2016 to software for companies in the home-buying process, and expanded into insurance from 2021. Porch Group's annual report for 2025 describes the company as a new kind of homeowners insurance company, with segments for insurance services, software and data, consumer services (home warranties and moving) and a reciprocal insurance exchange that Porch manages.

Contractor leads are now a small part of the picture. Porch.com's homepage sells home insurance, warranties and moving help and does not promote finding a contractor, and the 2025 annual report does not describe a contractor lead marketplace. Porch still runs a pro sign-up page and publishes Terms of Use for Pros (effective October 23, 2025) for its Porch Professional Network, and Porch Group's website lists Porch.com under contractors, saying it helps home professionals find jobs.

Under those terms, a Network Pro buys the right to contact homeowners who asked to be contacted about a particular project (a project request). You choose a subscription or pay-as-you-go. Porch says the cost to respond to a project request varies by service type and other factors and may be adjusted from time to time. Once you buy a request you generally cannot reject or return it, and Porch does not guarantee that a homeowner will hire you. Lead credits expire three months after they are issued. Subscriptions renew automatically, and to cancel you must notify Porch at least 15 days before the last day of the term (7 days for weekly or biweekly billing).

The trade-off: Porch does not publish lead prices or say how many pros can buy the same request, and its consumer site no longer promotes contractor matching, so request volume in your trade and area is an open question. Get the per-request price, the subscription term and the cancellation date in writing before you sign up.
platforms.how_it_works: Homeowners submit a project request and ask to be contacted by a pro. Porch delivers requests to Network Pros by email, a phone connection, its communications platform or other means. You buy the right to respond to a request, either one request at a time (pay-as-you-go) or through a subscription, and Porch sets the price by service type and other factors. A purchased request generally cannot be returned. Porch may run a background check for some programs and requires pros to hold any licenses, insurance and bonding their work requires.

platforms.tagline: Cost-per-click ads in Yelp search results and on competitor pages, plus Request-a-Quote inquiries for services businesses
platforms.typical_cost: Budget you set: Yelp says as little as $5 a day on average; ads are priced per click through an automated auction; no term contracts for self-serve advertisers

platforms.long_description:
Yelp Ads are the paid placements sold by Yelp Inc. (NYSE: YELP), which says it was founded in San Francisco in 2004 and is still based there. Yelp says users have contributed over 330 million reviews and that it had 510,000 paying advertising locations as of the second quarter of 2026. Its annual report says Yelp primarily sells performance-based ads, matched to consumers through an automated auction and priced on a cost-per-click basis.

The mechanics: you set a budget (Yelp says you can spend as little as $5 a day on average) and can change it whenever you want. Ads appear in the Sponsored Results sections above and below organic search results and on competitor pages, and Yelp says they also run on and off Yelp through its audience network. You target by location and keyword, pick a goal (calls, messages, website visits or directions), and write the ad yourself or let Yelp's algorithms optimize it. For services businesses, Yelp's Request-a-Quote feature lets consumers ask for quotes, and several businesses can respond with competing quotes.

Contracts and sales calls are where Yelp's reputation problems sit. Yelp's ads page says there are no term contracts with self-serve advertisers and you are free to cancel at any time, but Yelp also sells through local sales representatives. In 2024 Yelp paid $15 million to settle Gruber v. Yelp, a California Invasion of Privacy Act class action over recording its sales representatives' side of calls without notice; Yelp admitted no liability. The long-running complaint that Yelp hides non-advertisers' good reviews was tested in Levitt v. Yelp, where the Ninth Circuit in 2014 dismissed extortion claims without finding that any manipulation occurred.

The trade-off: you pay for clicks, not jobs, and Yelp does not publish cost-per-click ranges by trade or city. Buy through the self-serve platform if you want the no-term, cancel-anytime terms, set a daily budget you can afford to test with, and track which clicks turn into calls and booked work.
platforms.how_it_works: Set up a Yelp Ads campaign for your Yelp business page through the self-serve platform or with a Yelp sales representative. Choose a budget (Yelp says as little as $5 a day on average), locations, keywords and a goal such as calls, messages, website visits or directions. Yelp's automated auction places your ad in Sponsored Results above and below organic search results, on competitor pages and across its audience network, and ads are priced per click. Customers contact you by phone, message or Request-a-Quote. Yelp says self-serve advertisers have no term contract and can cancel at any time.

pros_detail.explanation: Yelp says you can spend as little as $5 a day on average and adjust your budget to any maximum, whenever and as often as you want.

pros_detail.title: No term contract on self-serve
pros_detail.explanation: Yelp's ads page says there are no term contracts with self-serve advertisers and you are free to cancel at any time without penalty.

pros_detail.title: Placement on competitor pages
pros_detail.explanation: Yelp says ads appear in Sponsored Results above and below organic results and on competitor pages, so you can reach people looking at other businesses in your category.

pros_detail.title: Request-a-Quote and lead tools for services businesses
pros_detail.explanation: Consumers can request quotes and services businesses can respond with competing quotes. Yelp's annual report also describes AI tools for services businesses, such as Yelp Receptionist, which asks project questions and helps qualify new leads.

cons_detail.title: You pay for clicks, not jobs
cons_detail.explanation: Yelp prices ads per click through an automated auction. A click is not a call or a booked job, so track results from the first week.

cons_detail.title: No published click prices
cons_detail.explanation: Yelp does not publish cost-per-click ranges by trade or city, so you learn what clicks cost only once a campaign is running.

cons_detail.title: Sales-call settlement
cons_detail.explanation: In 2024 Yelp paid $15 million to settle Gruber v. Yelp, a California class action over recording its sales representatives' side of calls without notice. Yelp admitted no liability or wrongdoing.

cons_detail.title: Rep-sold packages may differ from self-serve terms
cons_detail.explanation: The no-term, cancel-anytime language on Yelp's ads page applies to self-serve advertisers. If a sales representative offers a package with a commitment, get the length and cancellation terms in writing.

cons_detail.title: Competing quotes on Request-a-Quote
cons_detail.explanation: Request-a-Quote lets several services businesses send quotes to the same consumer, so you compete on response speed and price.

cons_detail.title: Review-filtering complaints persist
cons_detail.explanation: Business owners have alleged in court that Yelp hides positive reviews of non-advertisers. In Levitt v. Yelp (2014) the Ninth Circuit dismissed the extortion claims without finding that manipulation occurred, and Yelp's filtering, as described in that case, affects both positive and negative reviews.

platforms.best_team_size: Any size (budget-based, not per user)
platforms.weaknesses: Pay-per-click with no published click prices, a $15 million settlement over recording sales calls, rep-sold packages that may carry terms self-serve does not, and persistent but unproven complaints about review filtering
platforms.reputation_flag: Yelp paid $15 million to settle a California class action over recording its own sales representatives' side of sales calls without notice to the people called. The case (Gruber v. Yelp, San Francisco Superior Court, No. CGC-16-554784) was filed in October 2016 under the California Invasion of Privacy Act; the court granted final approval on April 10, 2024, and Yelp's annual report says the settlement involved no admission of liability or wrongdoing. Yelp's ads page says there are no term contracts with self-serve advertisers and you are free to cancel at any time; if a sales representative pitches a term commitment, get the length and cancellation terms in writing first. The long-running claim that Yelp hides non-advertisers' good reviews has not been established in court: in Levitt v. Yelp (2014) the Ninth Circuit dismissed extortion claims, holding that review manipulation, assuming it occurred, was not extortion, without finding that it did occur.

platform_faqs.q: Is Yelp Ads worth it?
platform_faqs.a: It depends on whether your customers search Yelp in your area. Start with a small self-serve budget (Yelp says as little as $5 a day on average), track calls, messages and booked jobs from ad clicks for a few weeks, and stop if clicks do not turn into work. Self-serve ads have no term contract.

platform_faqs.q: Do I have to sign a contract?
platform_faqs.a: Not for self-serve. Yelp's ads page says there are no term contracts with self-serve advertisers and you are free to cancel at any time. If a sales representative pitches a package with a commitment, get the term and cancellation rules in writing before you agree.

platform_faqs.q: What was the Yelp sales-call lawsuit?
platform_faqs.a: Gruber v. Yelp was a class action filed in San Francisco Superior Court in October 2016 under the California Invasion of Privacy Act over Yelp recording its own sales representatives' side of calls without notice. Yelp settled for $15 million, the court granted final approval on April 10, 2024, and Yelp admitted no liability or wrongdoing.

platform_faqs.q: Does Yelp hide reviews if I don't advertise?
platform_faqs.a: Business owners have alleged this for years, but it has not been proven in court. In Levitt v. Yelp (2014) the Ninth Circuit dismissed extortion claims, holding that review manipulation, assuming it occurred, was not extortion. As described in that case, Yelp's automated filtering affects both positive and negative reviews.

platforms.long_description:
Modernize is the home improvement lead brand of QuinStreet, Inc. (Nasdaq: QNST), a performance marketing company based in Foster City, California. QuinStreet completed its acquisition of Modernize on July 1, 2020, and its annual report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026 lists Modernize, Inc. as a subsidiary. QuinStreet calls Modernize the flagship brand of its home services business. Modernize is not part of Angi Inc. or IAC and is a separate company from HomeAdvisor.

QuinStreet says its home services business covers more than 15 trades and service areas, such as solar, windows, air conditioning, roofing and siding, plus bathrooms and kitchens, new and replacement gutters and home security, and that it serves over 1,000 clients a year. Inquiries come from QuinStreet's owned and operated websites, and QuinStreet sells contractors four formats: calls that connect consumers directly with a contractor's sales team, qualified inquiries, click listings and branded media. In January 2026 QuinStreet also bought HomeBuddy, another marketplace that connects homeowners with contractors.

We could not confirm Modernize's lead prices, how many contractors receive each inquiry, or its policy for returning bad leads from a primary source, so ask for all three in writing. QuinStreet's annual report says it is generally paid per click, per lead or per other action, so expect to pay for each delivered inquiry or call rather than for jobs won. Modernize's BBB profile, which lists an Austin, Texas address, shows 278 complaints closed in the last three years.

The trade-off: Modernize's trades are high-consideration replacement and remodeling projects rather than repair calls, and you pay for inquiries or calls whether or not they turn into jobs. Before you commit, get the price per lead or call, whether leads are shared, the return rules and any minimum spend in writing, and track your close rate by lead source.
platforms.how_it_works: Homeowners researching projects such as solar, windows, roofing, air conditioning, siding or remodeling fill out forms on QuinStreet's owned and operated websites, including Modernize. QuinStreet delivers the resulting inquiries, live calls that connect the consumer with your sales team, or click listings to participating contractors, and it also sells branded media. QuinStreet says it is generally paid per click, per lead or per other action. You contact the homeowner, quote the job and close the sale yourself.

pros_detail.explanation: QuinStreet says the business serves trades such as solar, windows, air conditioning, roofing and siding, plus bathrooms and kitchens, gutters and home security, which it describes as high-value, high-consideration home segments.

pros_detail.title: Several ways to buy
pros_detail.explanation: QuinStreet sells home services clients calls, inquiries, clicks and branded media, so you can choose live calls over form leads if your team closes better on the phone.

pros_detail.title: Public-company owner
pros_detail.explanation: Modernize has been part of QuinStreet, a Nasdaq-listed performance marketing company, since July 1, 2020, and QuinStreet's 2026 annual report lists Modernize, Inc. as a subsidiary.

platforms.long_description:
HomeAdvisor is one of the home services brands of Angi Inc. (Nasdaq: ANGI), which is based in Denver and says it operates the Angi, Angie's List, HomeAdvisor and Handy brands. Angi Inc. was formed in 2017 by combining IAC's HomeAdvisor business with Angie's List, and IAC spun off its stake on March 31, 2025. The FTC's complaint named HomeAdvisor, Inc., also doing business as Angi Leads and HomeAdvisor Powered by Angi. This review leads with the FTC action because it concerns how HomeAdvisor sold leads to pros.

The FTC action is one matter (FTC matter 1923106, Docket No. 9407). In March 2022 the FTC filed an administrative complaint charging that since at least mid-2014 HomeAdvisor made false, misleading or unsubstantiated claims about the quality and source of its leads and about how often they turn into jobs, and that sales agents misrepresented an optional one-month mHelpDesk subscription, which cost $59.99, as free. In January 2023 the FTC announced a consent order requiring HomeAdvisor to pay up to $7.2 million and barring those claims; the Commission finalized the order in April 2023, and in November 2023 the FTC said it had returned more than $3 million to businesses that paid for HomeAdvisor memberships.

How it works for pros today, according to Angi's annual report for 2025: after meeting eligibility criteria, pros buy service and are referred to consumers by Angi's algorithm, and lead fees are charged for consumer matches regardless of whether the pro ends up doing the job. In 2025 pros could buy full-priced leads within a monthly budget, discounted leads in a subscription package, double opt-in leads a la carte, or pre-priced offerings. A basic annual membership includes a business profile on HomeAdvisor.com and Angi.com, a mobile app and online tools. The FTC's January 2023 announcement said service providers generally paid an annual membership fee of $287.99 plus a separate fee for each lead; current prices are not published on the pages we could read.

Service professionals have also sued. In re HomeAdvisor, Inc. Litigation, a class action filed in federal court in Colorado in 2016 by pros who paid for HomeAdvisor memberships, alleges deceptive lead practices. In January 2024 the court refused to certify the nationwide and state deceptive-practices classes and certified only narrower classes over the use of former members' names and likenesses; in September 2024 it granted HomeAdvisor summary judgment on eight counts, and in March 2025 it denied the plaintiffs leave to file a second class-certification motion.

The trade-off: you pay a membership plus lead fees whether or not you win the work, you compete with other pros for each request, and the FTC order shows how its leads were sold to pros in the past. We do not recommend making it your first lead source; if you try it, set a monthly lead budget and get every price in writing.

platforms.long_description:
Bark is an online services marketplace founded in the UK in 2014 by Kai Feller and Andrew Michael and headquartered in London. Its careers site says it launched in the US in 2017 and also operates in Canada, Ireland, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Germany and France. Private equity firm EMK Capital acquired a majority stake from the founders and shareholders in 2022 and lists Bark as a current portfolio company. Bark covers far more than home services (business services, events, lessons and more), so trade requests sit alongside many other categories.

The model is pay to respond. A customer posts a request, pros who cover that service and area see it, and a pro who wants the job spends credits to respond. Bark says the credit cost depends on the service, the value of the job and local supply and demand; paying unlocks the customer's phone number and email, and further messages are free. Bark's terms say a maximum of five professionals will contact the customer on a general request, so every lead is shared.

The refund rules are narrow. Under Bark's terms, credits are refunded only if you report within 7 days that the phone number you received is invalid or the email address bounces. The first starter pack carries a one-time Get Hired Guarantee: if it produces no customer contract, Bark adds the same number of credits back to your account (credits, not cash). Credits bought on or after 1 November 2025 expire after 3 months, and expired credits are not refunded or extended. An optional Elite Pro subscription with recurring payments is also offered.

The trade-off: Bark requires no subscription and takes no commission on the job, but you pay before you know whether the customer will answer, you share each request with up to four other pros, and refunds cover only dead phone numbers or bounced emails. If you test it, set a fixed budget, track cost per hired job, and report invalid contact details inside the 7-day window.

Bark's terms say a maximum of five professionals will contact the customer on a general request. platforms.long_description:
eLocal is a pay-per-call lead network run by eLocal USA LLC from Conshohocken, Pennsylvania. It says it has connected consumers with service providers since 2008 and now serves home services alongside legal, medical, insurance, automotive and financial advertisers. UK-based HomeServe acquired eLocal in 2019, and eLocal says it and HomeServe were acquired by Brookfield in 2023. eLocal says it transfers more than 11 million calls a year.

The model is pay for performance. When you set up your program you make an initial deposit, which eLocal draws down only when it sends you a valid call or lead. eLocal generates demand through search engines and partners, then transfers live calls to your business number or sends form leads by email or text. eLocal says live calls are always exclusive to one business; form leads can be exclusive or shared, and its help center says a shared lead goes to as many as four other businesses in the area. eLocal advertises no contracts, no subscriptions and no commitments, and you can pause your account for up to seven days a month from the billing tab.

Read the billing rules before you start. Under eLocal's help center, a call counts as valid if it is in your service area and category and comes from a potential new customer, even if it goes unanswered, reaches voicemail, gets a busy signal or the caller is told they will be called back. Wrong numbers, job seekers and out-of-area or out-of-category calls are invalid. Price shoppers, estimate requests, scheduling needs you cannot meet, commercial or new-construction jobs, subcontract requests and calls you resold are not eligible for credit.

The trade-off: eLocal gives you exclusive live calls with no contract or subscription, but prices are not published, missed calls are billable, and shared form leads mean competing with other shops. Answer every call, set your service area, hours and categories carefully, and track cost per booked job.

You are charged only when a valid call or lead is sent. Live calls are always exclusive; form leads can be exclusive or shared with up to four other businesses. Calls are judged on the recorded conversation, and you can request credits for invalid calls such as wrong numbers, job seekers, or calls outside your area, category or business hours. You can pause your account for up to seven days a month.

platforms.long_description:
Networx is a home-improvement lead marketplace run by Networx Systems, Inc., which lists an Atlanta, Georgia address on its BBB profile. Networx says it finds homeowners through paid marketing such as Google, SEO, word of mouth, social media and content, and that it also partners with affiliates and third parties to meet demand. Its BBB profile lists categories from HVAC, plumbing, electrical and roofing to painting, flooring, landscaping, cleaning and pest control.

There are two main plans. On Pay Per Lead, the default shared plan, each lead goes to up to 4 contractors in total and arrives by text and email; Networx says these leads cost less than exclusive ones and go through the same screening. On Exclusive Leads, each lead goes to you alone, and during business hours Networx tries to call the homeowner to verify the request and transfer it to you as a live call. Networx's help center puts prices at about $10-$100+ per shared lead and $15-$120+ per exclusive lead, depending on the job type. Opportunity Leads can also be bought separately, and a Direct Calls add-on places your business in Google results with a weekly budget of $200-$500.

Billing is usually prepaid: you set a monthly, weekly or bi-weekly budget, each delivered lead is deducted, and the budget renews on your billing date. Networx says there are no contracts and no set-up fees, though its billing article says post-pay accounts pay an activation fee. Its contractor-leads marketing page instead describes "a small flat fee per month" with no registration or cancellation fees, so ask Networx which billing applies to your account before you sign up. Its lead credit policy covers disconnected numbers or fake contact details, jobs or areas you did not sign up for, duplicates and job seekers, and requests must be made within 14 days. A homeowner who already hired someone, is hesitant or is price shopping, or a bid you lost, does not qualify for credit.

The trade-off: Networx offers broad trade coverage, published price ranges and no contract, but shared leads go to up to four contractors, credit is limited to clearly bad leads, and its BBB profile lists 100 complaints closed in the last three years. Start with a small budget, respond fast, request credits within the 14-day window, and track cost per booked job before scaling.

On the shared Pay Per Lead plan each lead goes to up to 4 contractors by text and email. On the Exclusive Leads plan the lead goes only to you, and during business hours Networx tries to verify the homeowner by phone and transfer the call to you. You can pause your account, change your budget from the dashboard, and request credit within 14 days for leads with fake contact details, the wrong service or area, duplicates or job seekers.

platforms.long_description:
Nextdoor is a neighborhood social network run by Nextdoor Holdings, Inc., a San Francisco company listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker NXDR. Its annual report for 2025 says the platform reached 1 in 3 US households and had 21.0 million weekly active users as of December 31, 2025. Neighbors use it for local news and recommendations, and businesses can claim a free Business Page and buy ads.

For a trades business, the relevant product is self-serve advertising. Nextdoor says local businesses choose one of three goals (more website visits, promoting a sale or discount as a Local Deal, or getting more messages), set a radius of up to 30 miles around the business, which Nextdoor turns into a set of ZIP codes, and then set a daily budget and duration or pick one of three recommended starter plans that recur. Nextdoor says the audience you select has no impact on the cost of the ad, and you can pause and resume an ad at any time. Its business site also describes targeting in Ads Manager by homeownership, household income, age, gender and interests, plus custom audiences for retargeting.

Nextdoor sells ads, not leads. Your ad sends neighbors to your website, your deal or your inbox, and turning that into booked jobs depends on your offer, your creative and how fast you follow up. Competitors can advertise in the same ZIP codes, and someone scrolling a neighborhood feed is usually not searching for a contractor at that moment, so intent is generally lower than with a search ad.

The trade-off: Nextdoor gives a local trades business a low-commitment way to put its name in front of nearby households, with a budget you set yourself and no per-lead fee, but it is an ad channel you have to manage. Pair it with search-based channels for people who are already looking for a contractor, and treat Nextdoor as local presence rather than a lead supply.
platforms.how_it_works: With a free Business Page, you create an ad in Nextdoor's self-serve Ads Manager. Choose a goal (website visits, a Local Deal promoting a sale or discount, or more messages), set a radius of up to 30 miles around your business (Nextdoor highlights the ZIP codes it covers), then set a daily budget and duration or pick one of Nextdoor's three recommended starter plans, which run on a recurring basis. Add payment and publish; Nextdoor says ads go through a quick approval before going live. You can pause and resume an ad at any time. Neighbors who respond visit your site, redeem your deal or message you, and the follow-up is yours.

platforms.name: EnergySage
platforms.tagline: Clean-energy comparison marketplace where vetted installers quote homeowners who compare offers side by side
platforms.typical_cost: Not published. Free for homeowners; EnergySage says installers pay a small fee to join its marketplace after it vets them, and its terms say it may receive a fee from installers for the opportunity to respond to shoppers' requests. Ask EnergySage for current installer terms.
platforms.exclusivity: Shared: homeowners receive and compare several installer quotes side by side
platforms.long_description:
EnergySage is an online marketplace where homeowners compare quotes for home solar and, on its consumer site, batteries, heat pumps and EV charging. It was founded by Vikram Aggarwal, is based in Boston, and says it built its marketplace with funding from the US Department of Energy. Schneider Electric bought a controlling stake in February 2022, and EnergySage said then that it would continue to operate independently. EnergySage says more than 1.5 million people have shopped with it and 60,000 homeowners have gone solar with it.

For an installer, it is a source of homeowners who are already comparing offers. EnergySage says it pre-screens installers for more than two years of experience installing solar PV, solar PV licensing and insurance, a reputation for customer service and quality installations, and high-quality equipment at good value. Its installer page says approved companies get access to solar shoppers plus sales training, workflow tools, a dedicated partner success manager and market data.

EnergySage does not publish installer pricing. Its about page says installers pay a small fee to join the marketplace after EnergySage vets them, and its terms of use say it may receive a fee from installers for the opportunity to respond to shoppers' requests. Homeowners use the site for free and compare quotes side by side, so each opportunity is shared with other installers and your price sits next to your competitors' prices.

The trade-off: the homeowners are in-market and the platform does the comparison work for them, but that same comparison puts your price next to other vetted installers. It suits established solar and electrification installers who can win on value and fast, professional follow-up; installers who want uncontested leads should use it alongside their own marketing rather than instead of it.
platforms.how_it_works: A homeowner enters a ZIP code and builds a profile on EnergySage, free of charge. Installers that EnergySage has vetted and approved respond with quotes, which the homeowner compares side by side, with help from EnergySage's Energy Advisors if they want it, before choosing an installer. EnergySage says installers pay a fee to join after vetting, and its terms say installers may pay for the opportunity to respond to requests; it does not publish the amounts. Winning depends on your price, equipment, reviews and how quickly and professionally you respond.

platforms.name: Meta Lead Ads
platforms.tagline: Facebook and Instagram lead ads: target your service area and collect contact details through forms prefilled from people's accounts
platforms.typical_cost: Self-serve auction with no set price: you set a campaign budget, and Meta bills lead-generation campaigns on impressions, not per lead. Your cost per lead depends on your market, audience, budget and offer.
platforms.exclusivity: Your own ads and forms: each lead comes only to you, but competitors can target the same audience
platforms.long_description:
Meta Lead Ads are the lead-generation ads on Facebook and Instagram, run by Meta Platforms, Inc. of Menlo Park, California. Instead of sending someone to your website, the ad can open an instant form with the person's contact details already filled in from their account, so a homeowner can ask for a quote in a couple of taps; Meta says the details are not sent to the business until the person taps submit. Facebook introduced lead ads in 2015, and Meta now also offers website forms and chat-based lead ads across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its other apps.

The strengths are targeting and low friction. You choose a service area and audience, and you can build Custom Audiences from your customer list or from website visitors tracked with the Meta Pixel, plus Lookalike Audiences of people similar to your customers. Meta also offers lead verification by SMS passcode and work email for businesses that want fewer but more serious leads. Leads can be downloaded from Meta's Leads Center or sent to a CRM in real time through integrations or webhooks.

Intent is the weak point. A Meta lead tapped a form while scrolling, not while searching for a plumber, so fewer of them are ready to hire, and a form that takes two taps also invites casual submissions. Call back quickly, add qualifying questions, and track which leads turn into jobs. Meta bills lead-generation campaigns on impressions and publishes no set prices, so your real cost per job depends on your targeting, offer and close rate.

The trade-off: Meta Lead Ads can produce leads at scale and are useful for retargeting past visitors and customers, but the leads need fast follow-up and filtering and are usually less ready to buy than search leads. Use them alongside search-based channels rather than instead of them.
platforms.how_it_works: In Meta Ads Manager, create a campaign with the leads objective, set your budget, service area and audience (including Custom or Lookalike Audiences), and choose a lead format such as an instant form, a website form or chat. With an instant form, the person's contact details are filled in from their account, and nothing reaches you until they tap submit. Leads arrive in Meta's Leads Center, where you can download them, or flow into your CRM through an integration or webhooks. Meta bills lead-generation campaigns on impressions in an auction, so what you pay per lead depends on your audience, budget and offer. Follow up fast: these are people who were scrolling, not searching.

cons_detail.explanation: A Meta lead filled in a form while scrolling, not while searching for a service, so fewer are ready to hire than with search-based channels.

cons_detail.explanation: People who submitted a form while scrolling lose interest quickly, so you need a way to call or text them back promptly.

cons_detail.explanation: Two-tap forms invite casual or mistaken submissions; qualifying questions and verification help, but they also reduce volume.

cons_detail.explanation: You or an agency must build the creative, forms, targeting and follow-up. Run without discipline, it produces cheap leads that do not turn into jobs.

cons_detail.explanation: Meta bills on impressions in an auction and publishes no rates, so cost per lead and per job varies and has to be tracked.

platforms.best_team_size: 2-100 users
platforms.weaknesses: Leads are lower-intent than search, need fast follow-up and screening, and cost varies with an auction Meta does not price in advance. It rewards businesses that manage creative, targeting and follow-up carefully, and works best alongside search-based channels.

platform_faqs.a: They are the lead-generation ads on Facebook and Instagram. Instead of sending people to a website, the ad can open an instant form prefilled with the person's contact details from their account, so they can ask for a quote in a couple of taps. Meta also offers website forms and chat-based lead ads. Facebook introduced lead ads in 2015.

platform_faqs.q: Are Meta Lead Ads good for contractors?
platform_faqs.a: They can be, for lead volume, retargeting and local awareness, if you follow up fast and screen leads. The people who respond were scrolling rather than searching, so they are usually less ready to hire than search leads. Most contractors are better off using them alongside search-based channels.

platform_faqs.a: There is no set price. You set a budget and Meta runs an auction; for lead-generation campaigns Meta bills on impressions, not per lead. Your cost per lead depends on your market, audience and offer, so track the cost per booked job, not only the cost per lead.

platform_faqs.a: The people who respond were scrolling, not searching for help, and a two-tap form invites casual submissions. Tight targeting, qualifying questions, Meta's SMS or work email verification, a clear offer and a fast callback all help.

platforms.name: TaskRabbit

In California and Massachusetts, invoices show only a Service Fee.
platforms.exclusivity: Clients choose you directly: they pick a Tasker by price, skills and reviews, and you set your own hourly rate
platforms.long_description:
TaskRabbit is an on-demand marketplace that connects people who need help with household tasks, such as furniture assembly, TV mounting, moving help, cleaning, yard work and home repairs, with local Taskers. It was founded in Boston in 2008 by Leah and Kevin Busque, is now based in San Francisco, and has been owned by Ingka Group (IKEA) since 2017. TaskRabbit says it operates in thousands of cities across eight countries, including the United States. In July 2026 it rebranded Dolly, the delivery platform it bought in 2024, as Taskrabbit Delivery for big-and-bulky moving, hauling and delivery work.

The key point for this directory is who it is for. TaskRabbit is built for individual Taskers, who work as independent contractors, not for trade companies with crews and trucks. To register you must be at least 18, pass an identity check and a criminal background check, and have a smartphone and a checking account for direct deposit. Taskers set their own hourly rates and can set a two-hour minimum instead of the platform's one-hour minimum; clients choose a Tasker by price, skills and reviews and can book as early as the same day.

The economics are gig-platform economics. TaskRabbit says Taskers pay a one-time, non-refundable $25 registration fee and that beyond it, all fees are charged to clients, not Taskers. Clients pay a Service Fee and a Trust & Support fee on top of the Tasker's rate, each calculated as a percentage of the hourly rate; in California and Massachusetts, invoices show only a Service Fee. Taskers keep 100% of tips. Bookings, invoices and payments run through the platform, and the work skews toward small hourly jobs rather than larger projects.

The trade-off: for a solo handyman or odd-job worker, TaskRabbit supplies small-task work with no marketing spend beyond the registration fee, but it is a gig platform for individuals, not a lead source for a trades company. Established plumbing, HVAC or electrical businesses should look at lead and advertising channels built for companies instead.
platforms.how_it_works: Download the Tasker app and register as an individual: you must be at least 18, pass an identity check and a criminal background check, and add a checking account for direct deposit. Once your registration is processed, you pay a one-time, non-refundable $25 registration fee. You choose your task categories, set your hourly rates and availability, and can set a two-hour minimum. Clients choose a Tasker by price, skills and reviews and can book as early as the same day. After the task you submit an invoice through the platform within 24 hours; clients pay your rate plus TaskRabbit's Service Fee and Trust & Support fee, and you keep 100% of any tips.

Its provider agreement also lets it charge administrative or service fees, such as payment processor fees, directly or by withholding them from provider pay.
platforms.exclusivity: Platform-assigned jobs: LawnStarter prices each job and offers it to providers, and it retains ownership of the customer
platforms.long_description:
LawnStarter is an app-based lawn-care marketplace based in Austin, Texas. It says it was founded in 2013 as an Austin startup, is led by CEO and co-founder Steven Corcoran, and now works in 500+ cities with 7,500 providers it calls LawnTrepreneurs, offering 30+ services. LawnStarter acquired Lawn Love, another lawn-care marketplace, in 2021, and Lawn Love providers sign the same LawnStarter, Inc. provider agreement. Homeowners get a set price from LawnStarter's satellite and AI measuring, book online and pay by card, and LawnStarter routes the work to local providers.

For a provider, it is routed demand with no marketing. LawnStarter's page for lawn-care businesses says it prices each lawn with its own software based on square footage and other factors, providers see job offers in an app and pick the recurring jobs that suit them, with no bidding, and pay arrives by weekly Stripe deposit at the amount shown on the offer. It says providers pay nothing to use the service and that LawnStarter keeps a small portion of the mowing price. Stated requirements are a mower, string trimmer and leaf blower, a truck or SUV, authorization to work in the US and passing a background check.

The provider agreement is where the trade-offs sit. Once you accept an order you cannot change the fee unless LawnStarter agrees in writing, LawnStarter may charge administrative or service fees such as payment processor fees or withhold them from your pay, and the agreement says LawnStarter will retain ownership of the customers. During the agreement and for one year after it ends, you may not solicit or accept business from customers connected to you through LawnStarter, except customers you served before or acquired independently, with a $5,000 penalty per violation. You must also carry adequate insurance naming LawnStarter as an additional insured. On the consumer side, BBB rates LawnStarter F and lists 329 complaints closed in the last three years (checked 30 September 2026).

The trade-off: LawnStarter can fill a route quickly with no marketing spend, but you work at prices it sets, it keeps the customer relationship, and the non-solicitation clause limits taking those customers with you. Use it to fill capacity while building a customer base you own through your own marketing.
platforms.how_it_works: A homeowner enters an address; LawnStarter measures the lawn with its satellite and AI technology, shows a set price, and takes the booking and card payment. LawnStarter then offers the job to local providers in its app. Providers pick the recurring jobs they want, see the pay on each offer before accepting, do the work, and are paid by weekly Stripe deposit. LawnStarter sets the customer price, keeps a portion, and retains ownership of the customer under its provider agreement; once you accept an order, you cannot change the fee without LawnStarter's written agreement.

platform_faqs.q: How does LawnStarter pricing work for providers?
platform_faqs.a: LawnStarter prices each lawn with its own software based on square footage and other factors, then offers the job to providers in its app. You see the pay before accepting and are paid that amount by weekly Stripe deposit. LawnStarter says it keeps a small portion of the mowing price, and its agreement lets it charge or withhold service fees such as payment processor fees.

platform_faqs.q: What is LawnStarter's BBB rating?
platform_faqs.a: BBB rates LawnStarter F and lists it as not accredited, with 329 complaints closed in the last three years as of 30 September 2026. A BBB rating reflects complaint history and how complaints were handled; BBB says it does not include customer reviews.

platform_faqs.q: Can I keep customers I serve through LawnStarter?
platform_faqs.a: No. The provider agreement says LawnStarter retains ownership of the customers and bars you from soliciting or accepting business from customers connected to you through the platform during the agreement and for one year after it ends, except customers you served before or acquired independently, with a $5,000 penalty per violation.

platforms.name: GreenPal
platforms.tagline: Lawn-care marketplace where pros bid their own prices for recurring mowing clients, for a 5% fee on each successful payment
platforms.typical_cost: Free for homeowners. GreenPal charges vendors 5% when a customer's payment for a completed service succeeds, including tips and approved additional charges but excluding sales tax, with no signup, bidding or monthly fee. Card processing through the vendor's own Stripe account is separate (Stripe's standard US card rate is 2.9% + $0.30). Vendors set their own prices.
platforms.exclusivity: Competitive bids: local vendors bid their own prices on each lawn, and the homeowner picks one
platforms.long_description:
GreenPal is a lawn-care marketplace run by GreenPal Co. of Nashville, Tennessee. Homeowners get prices from local lawn-care businesses, compare them and book one, free of charge. GreenPal's team page names Bryan Clayton, a former landscape-company owner, as CEO, with Gene Caballero and Zach Hendrix. GreenPal says 85,447 lawn-care businesses use it and that participating vendors have served 802,584 clients, with $132,400,015 in gross service payments recorded through vendor accounts as of September 30, 2026.

The model leaves pricing with the provider. GreenPal's terms say vendors determine the price for their services, and vendors bid on lawns in their area, with several free bid opportunities a day. GreenPal says it charges vendors no signup, bidding or monthly fee; instead it takes 5% when a customer's payment for a completed service succeeds, including tips and approved additional charges but not sales tax. Payments run through the vendor's own Stripe account, and Stripe charges its own processing fees (its standard US card rate is 2.9% + $0.30) and controls payout timing. In GreenPal's example, the vendor keeps $45.75 of a $50 payment.

The work is recurring by design. GreenPal's help pages say vendors on the system take only weekly or every-two-week clients during the mowing season, and after each cut the homeowner gets an email with a photo of the lawn that serves as the invoice; the card is charged after the lawn is mowed. Homeowners compare several prices, so price and reviews decide who wins, and a new vendor without reviews may need to price keenly at first. Volume depends on how many homeowners and competing vendors are in your area.

The trade-off: GreenPal lets you set your own prices for a 5% fee plus card processing, unlike platforms that set the price for you, such as LawnStarter, but every job is won against competing bids and GreenPal's fee applies to every successful payment, tips included. It suits lawn-care businesses that want recurring mowing clients and are prepared to compete on price and reviews.
platforms.how_it_works: A homeowner requests lawn-care prices on GreenPal for free, and local vendors bid their own price. The homeowner compares the bids and books a vendor. Vendors on GreenPal take weekly or every-two-week clients during the mowing season; after each service the vendor uploads a completion photo, the homeowner receives it by email as the invoice, and the card is charged after the lawn is mowed. The payment goes through the vendor's own Stripe account; GreenPal takes 5% of each successful payment, including tips and approved additional charges, and Stripe takes its processing fee.

platform_faqs.q: How is GreenPal different from LawnStarter?
platform_faqs.a: On GreenPal, vendors set their own prices and bid for jobs; GreenPal takes 5% of each successful payment, and payments run through the vendor's own Stripe account. LawnStarter prices each job itself, offers it to providers at a set pay, and its provider agreement says LawnStarter retains ownership of the customers. GreenPal's model leaves more control over pricing with the provider.

platform_faqs.q: What does GreenPal cost lawn-care pros?
platform_faqs.a: GreenPal says there is no signup, bidding or monthly fee. It charges 5% when a customer's payment for a completed service succeeds, including tips and approved additional charges but not sales tax. Stripe charges its processing fee separately (2.9% + $0.30 on standard US cards). In GreenPal's example, you keep $45.75 of a $50 payment.

platform_faqs.q: Is GreenPal worth it for lawn-care providers?
platform_faqs.a: It can be for businesses that want recurring mowing clients at their own prices. The trade-offs are bid competition, the need for good reviews to win, and a fee that applies to every successful payment, tips included.

platform_faqs.q: Do I keep customers I win on GreenPal?
platform_faqs.a: You serve the client directly on a recurring weekly or every-two-week schedule at your own price, and payments run through your own Stripe account, with GreenPal taking 5% of each successful payment made through the platform. Check GreenPal's current vendor terms before moving any client off the platform.
